title: Strings as Data Sequences
learningObjectives: Explain strings as sequences of text units with language-specific details.
Use common string operations such as length, indexing, slicing, and searching.
Recognize that string indexing may operate on bytes, code units, code points, or grapheme clusters.
Describe why many string values are immutable in common languages.
Avoid unsafe assumptions about text length, encoding, and substring boundaries.

understand.concept: A string represents text as an ordered sequence. Many programming languages provide operations to inspect its length, access parts, search for text, concatenate, or transform it. However, the meaning of an index and the unit counted by a length operation can differ across languages and encodings.
understand.whyItMatters: Text processing is used for names, messages, identifiers, files, search, and user input. String operations can produce bugs when code assumes that each visible character occupies one simple index position.
understand.analogy: A string is like a line of printed symbols. You can find a word, take a section, or join another line—but a symbol's internal representation may not match the way a person sees it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not capture Unicode grapheme clusters, encoding, locale-specific operations, or language-specific mutability and indexing rules.

explain.narrative: Strings are sequences of text, but they are not necessarily arrays of user-perceived characters. Depending on the language, length and indexing may count bytes, code units, code points, or another unit. Common operations include concatenation, substring or slice, search, replacement, trimming, and case conversion. Some languages treat strings as immutable, so a transformation creates a new string. Use text-aware libraries when working with Unicode or locale-sensitive behavior.

commonMistakes: Assuming string length equals the count of visible characters for every text.
Using indexes without understanding the language's string indexing unit.
Confusing a search result or index with a boolean result.
Assuming strings can be changed in place in every language.
Ignoring encoding and locale when text includes multilingual characters.
